verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the interest rate where it is, at 1.25%. The BoJ only raised it six weeks ago, and two of its nine members already thought that rise was too soon. A rise is possible, but less likely.
verdict.confidence_note: “Medium” means we think Hold is clearly more likely, but not by a huge margin. Two price reports (October 23 and the morning of October 30), the yen and oil prices could still change our answer.
verdict.short_version: The BoJ has said many times that it will keep raising rates. The real question is how fast. In this cycle it has waited about three months or more between rises, and it raised only on September 18. We think it will more likely wait until December or later than act again in October.
verdict.card_why: The BoJ only raised six weeks ago on a split vote and has never moved at back-to-back meetings; national core inflation is 1.7%.

why_steps.title: The BoJ has one main job, and one main tool
why_steps.html: The BoJ's job is to keep prices steady. Its target is that things should cost about 2% more each year. For decades Japan had the opposite problem: prices barely moved or even fell, and the BoJ kept its interest rate at or below zero. Over the past few years that has changed, and prices now rise every year. Its main tool is its interest rate, the cost of borrowing money between banks overnight (officially the “uncollateralized overnight call rate”). Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. In Japan the BoJ is slowly taking its foot off the gas: even at 1.25%, it says interest rates are still low compared with inflation, so they still help the economy rather than hold it back.

why_steps.title: Right now, the price picture is confusing
why_steps.html: On the surface, prices look calm. In August, consumer prices without fresh food (the BoJ's main measure, often called “core CPI”) were up 1.7% on a year earlier, a little below the 2% goal (Statistics Bureau). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost ¥10,000 a year ago now costs about ¥10,170. The goal would be about ¥10,200. But underneath, pressure is building. A Middle East conflict pushed oil prices up this year (Board member Masu spoke of “the closure of the Strait of Hormuz”), and the yen is weak, at about ¥158 per US dollar. Together these make imports expensive: prices Japanese companies pay for imports were up 24.5% in yen terms in September, and prices companies charge each other were up 6.8% (BoJ). Household energy bills look cheap only because the government is helping: the BoJ says measures such as “fuel oil subsidies” and support for electricity and gas bills are holding consumer prices down this year (Outlook Report). Tokyo, whose figures come out first, already shows a jump: in September, prices without fresh food and energy were up 3.0% in Tokyo, from 2.0% in August (Statistics Bureau). Part of that jump came from changes in public fees such as nursery fees and water charges, not only from businesses raising prices.

why_steps.title: So the BoJ has been pressing the brake, step by step
why_steps.html: The BoJ raised its rate three times in the past year: to 0.75% in December 2025, to 1.0% in June 2026 and to 1.25% on September 18, 2026. Each time it waited at least about three months before the next rise. The September rise was not unanimous: the vote was 7–2. Member Asada Toichiro said core prices had recently been “below 2 percent” and the economy could not be called strong; member Sato Ayano said the economy and prices had not “substantially accelerated” (statement). At the same time, other members want to go faster. The BoJ's statement says it “will continue to raise the policy interest rate”, but gives no date. There are only two meetings left this year: October 30 and December 18. The question is whether the next rise comes now, or later.

why_steps.title: Reasons the BoJ might wait
why_steps.html:
• It just raised. September 18 was only six weeks before this meeting. In the past year the BoJ has never raised at two meetings in a row.
  • Two members already said “too soon” in September. Raising again straight away would deepen that split.
  • Consumer prices are below 2%. National core CPI was 1.7% in August, partly because of government energy support. The full national picture for September only arrives on October 23.
  • The economy is growing only slowly. It grew at a 1.4% yearly pace in spring, but household spending was flat and business investment fell 0.9% in the quarter (Cabinet Office). Big companies expect business conditions to get worse over the next three months (Tankan).
  • The Governor did not commit. Asked about rises at back-to-back meetings, Governor Ueda said the BoJ cannot promise in advance either way; it depends on the outlook and risks (press conference, Japanese).
  • The market already pressed the brake. The 10-year government bond rate is about 3%, up from a 2.67% average in June (FRED), so home loans and company borrowing have already become more expensive.

why_steps.title: Reasons the BoJ might raise in October anyway
why_steps.html:
• A forecast meeting. October is one of the four meetings each year with a new Outlook Report, which gives the BoJ a natural moment to explain a move.
  • Price pressure in the pipeline. Import prices up 24.5% and business prices up 6.8% usually reach shop shelves later. Member Takata warned that “the rise in producer prices upstream will likely spread to consumer prices downstream” (speech).
  • The weak yen. At about ¥158 per dollar, the yen makes imported food and fuel dearer. The BoJ says it does not target the yen, but it does say exchange rates affect prices.
  • Some members want speed. In September one view was that “If signs of an upward deviation in prices are observed, the Bank will need to accelerate the pace of rate hikes” (Summary of Opinions).
  • The BoJ expects inflation to rise now. Deputy Governor Himino said “CPI inflation will move up and stay above 2 percent in the second half of fiscal 2026”, which is October 2026 to March 2027 (speech).

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

left: Tokyo prices without fresh food and energy 3.0%
New forecasts due at this meeting
right: Two members voted against that rise

why_steps.html: Both sides have real arguments. What tips us toward Hold is timing: the BoJ has moved slowly and carefully all through this cycle, it only raised six weeks ago, and the vote was already split. Waiting until December costs it little, and by then it will have two more months of price data and the summer growth figures. That is why we say about 70% Hold and 27% Raise, with a small 3% chance of a cut, which would take a financial shock.

why_steps.title: The things to watch: two price reports and the yen
why_steps.html: On Friday, October 23 at 8:30 a.m. Japan time, the Statistics Bureau publishes national consumer prices for September. If core CPI (without fresh food) jumps to about 2.5% or more, and prices without fresh food and energy also rise clearly, we would move much closer to calling a Raise. A reading still below 2% would make us more confident in Hold. On Friday, October 30 at 8:30 a.m., a few hours before the decision, Tokyo prices for October come out. A further jump there would add to the case for a rise. Outside the data, a sharp fall in the yen well beyond ¥160 per dollar, or a new spike in oil, would also raise the chance of an October rise.

timeline.title: The BoJ held its rate at 0.5%, but two members wanted more
timeline.what: The BoJ kept its rate at 0.5% twice, both times by a 7–2 vote. Members Takata Hajime and Tamura Naoki voted against. Tamura proposed 0.75%, saying risks to prices were “more skewed to the upside.” In September the BoJ also decided to start slowly selling the stock funds (ETFs) it had bought in the past, at about ¥330 billion a year.
timeline.why: The short statements do not give the majority's reasons. The two dissenters argued that the 2% goal was more or less reached and that risks to prices were tilting upward.
timeline.people: Little changed. Loan and deposit rates stayed low, as they had for many years.
timeline.because: the BoJ kept watching wages; by December it said firms were highly likely to keep raising them.

timeline.title: The BoJ raised its rate to 0.75%
timeline.what: All members agreed to raise the rate by 0.25 points, to 0.75%. The BoJ said “it is highly likely that firms will continue to raise wages steadily next year.”
timeline.why: The BoJ judged that wages and prices were now rising together in a steady way. It also said “Real interest rates are expected to remain significantly negative” after the rise, meaning the rate was still below inflation.
timeline.people: Variable-rate home loans and business loans became a little more expensive. Bank deposits began to pay slightly more.
timeline.because: the BoJ paused to watch the effect, while some members already argued for the next step.

timeline.title: A pause at 0.75%
timeline.what: The BoJ held, by 8–1. Member Takata wanted 1.0%, arguing the 2% goal was largely met and that “risks to prices in Japan were skewed to the upside.”
timeline.why: The short statement does not give the majority's reasons. The BoJ had raised only a month earlier.
timeline.people: Not much change. Loan and deposit rates stayed about the same.
timeline.because: the BoJ was sitting still when a new problem arrived: conflict in the Middle East sent oil prices up.

timeline.title: An energy shock: oil jumps, and the board splits
timeline.what: The BoJ held at 0.75% twice. In March it noted “crude oil prices have risen significantly” (vote 8–1, Takata against). In April the vote was 6–3: Nakagawa Junko, Takata and Tamura all voted against. Tamura proposed 1.0%, seeing “risks to prices becoming significantly skewed to the upside.” New member Asada Toichiro joined the Board in April.
timeline.why: Japan imports nearly all of its oil. When oil gets expensive, so does fuel, shipping, farming and making things.
timeline.people: Fuel and electricity got more expensive, although government support kept part of the rise away from household bills.
timeline.because: with one-third of the Board asking for a rise, the next move looked close.

timeline.title: The BoJ raised its rate to 1.0%
timeline.what: The BoJ raised by 0.25 points, by a 7–1 vote. Member Asada voted against, judging that “downside risks to production and employment were greater than upside risks to prices.” The BoJ said “the rise in crude oil prices is expected to push up prices, mainly of energy and goods.”
timeline.why: Wages were still rising, and the BoJ saw a risk that underlying inflation could move above its goal as oil costs spread.
timeline.people: Variable-rate home loans and business loans rose a little again. Savings rates edged up.
timeline.because: the debate moved from “whether” to “how fast.”

timeline.title: A hold at 1.0%, and new forecasts
timeline.what: The BoJ held, by 8–1. Member Takata wanted 1.25%, saying “the situation had shifted to a new phase in which the Bank needs to adopt a nimble approach.” New forecasts put core inflation at 2.5% for fiscal 2026 and 2.4% for fiscal 2027, and growth at only 0.6% for fiscal 2026.
timeline.why: The BoJ lowered its fiscal 2026 inflation forecast (from 2.8% in April) mainly because of government measures to cut energy bills. It said spring wage talks delivered base pay rises of “around 3.5 percent.”
timeline.people: Pay was rising, but so were food and fuel costs. The government's energy support kept official inflation lower than many people felt it was.
timeline.because: the BoJ said it would keep raising rates, and markets watched for the next step after the summer.

timeline.title: Consumer prices calm, pipeline prices hot, jobs firm
timeline.what: National core CPI was up 1.7% in August (headline 1.9%). Wages were up 3.8% on a year earlier, and 1.5% after inflation. Unemployment was 2.5%, with 1.18 jobs on offer per job seeker.
timeline.people: Paychecks were rising faster than official prices, a welcome change after years of falling real pay.
timeline.because: the BoJ had to choose between the calm consumer numbers and the hot pipeline numbers.

timeline.title: The BoJ raised its rate to 1.25%
timeline.what: A rise of 0.25 points, by a 7–2 vote. Asada and Sato voted against. The BoJ said “underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2 percent” and that it “will continue to raise the policy interest rate.”
timeline.people: Variable loan rates rose again. Deposit rates edged up.
timeline.because: markets started asking how soon the next rise would come.

timeline.title: The yen weakened and bond rates stayed high
timeline.what: The yen moved from about ¥156 per dollar (Sep 17) to about ¥158 (Oct 9). The 10-year government bond rate was 3.03%–3.11% in early October; the 30-year rate was above 4%.
timeline.why: Even after the rise, Japan's rates are far below US rates, so money keeps flowing out of the yen. Oil also costs more in yen when the yen is weak.
timeline.people: Imported food, fuel and travel abroad got more expensive. Fixed-rate home loans, which follow long-term bond rates, are much dearer than a year ago.
timeline.because: the weak yen added price pressure, which strengthens the case for continuing to raise rates.

timeline.title: New signals: Tankan, Tokyo prices, and the Governor
timeline.what: Tokyo prices without fresh food and energy jumped to 3.0% in September. The BoJ's big business survey (Tankan) showed large manufacturers in a better mood, but big firms expect conditions to worsen. Business prices were up 6.8% and import prices 24.5% in September.
timeline.because: our reading is “raise again, but probably not yet”, which is why our main call is Hold.

choices.title: Hold: keep the rate at 1.25%
choices.meaning: the BoJ keeps its rate where it is and repeats that it will keep raising later. A hold here would be a “not yet”, not a “never”.
for: Only six weeks since the last rise. The BoJ has spaced its rises at least about three months apart in this cycle.
A split Board. Two members voted against the September rise.
National core CPI is 1.7%. That is below the 2% goal, even if government support is part of the reason.
Weak spending and investment. Household spending was flat and business investment fell in spring.
December offers more information: two more national price reports, the summer GDP figure (Nov 16) and the Tokyo November prices.
against: Pipeline pressure is strong. Import prices up 24.5% and business prices up 6.8% could push shop prices up soon.
The weak yen. If the yen keeps sliding, waiting gets riskier.
A hot September CPI on October 23 could make waiting feel too risky.
choices.everyday: loan and savings rates would stay roughly where they are for now. Attention would turn to December.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 1.5%
choices.meaning: the BoJ raises at two meetings in a row, which it has not done in the past year, to show it will not let rising import costs turn into lasting inflation.
for: New forecasts. October brings a new Outlook Report, a natural moment to explain a rise.
The BoJ expects inflation above 2% now. Deputy Governor Himino expects CPI inflation to “stay above 2 percent in the second half of fiscal 2026.”
Tokyo prices jumped. Prices without fresh food and energy reached 3.0% in September.
Hawkish members. Some members want to reach the rate goal “relatively soon” and to “accelerate the pace” if prices overshoot.
Yen and oil. The yen near ¥158 and Brent oil above $120 keep import costs high.
against: It would deepen the split. Two members already opposed the last rise.
Growth is slow. The BoJ itself forecast only 0.6% growth for fiscal 2026.
The Governor avoided any promise of back-to-back rises.
choices.everyday: variable-rate home loans and business loans would get a little more expensive again. Deposits would pay a bit more. A rise could also support the yen, which would make imports slightly cheaper.

choices.title: Cut: lower the rate
choices.meaning: the BoJ would reverse its September decision and press the gas.
for: Only in an emergency, such as a market crash or a sudden serious problem in the financial system.
Even then, the BoJ would more likely hold first than cut straight away.
against: The BoJ just raised and says it will keep raising.
Nobody on the Board is asking for it. In the statements and speeches we read, the most cautious members wanted to hold, not cut.
choices.everyday: loans would get slightly cheaper, but the surprise would likely signal that something had gone badly wrong, and the yen would probably fall.

change.lead: Our 70% / 27% / 3% guess is based on what we know today. New information arrives almost every day. Some of it can move our view a lot. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro: The BoJ can only react to information it has already seen. A report released before October 30 can change the October decision. A report released after it can only shape what happens in December. That is why the reports in the first part of the table matter most right now. All times are Japan Standard Time (JST), which is 13 hours ahead of US Eastern Time.

speech_by_board_member_koeda_k.why: One of the last public hints before the meeting.
speech_by_board_member_koeda_k.trigger: Clear support for a rise soon → leans Raise. Stress on patience → firms up Hold.

national_cpi.why: The most important report before the meeting. It shows whether Tokyo's September jump is spreading nationwide.
national_cpi.trigger: Core CPI about 2.5% or more → Raise becomes much more likely. Still below 2% → more confident in Hold.

services_producer_price_index.why: Shows whether costs are rising beyond goods and energy.
services_producer_price_index.trigger: A clear speed-up would add to the case for Raise.

indicators_for_core_cpi.why: The BoJ says its decisions depend on “underlying” inflation.
indicators_for_core_cpi.trigger: Measures at or above 2% → leans Raise.

tokyo_cpi.why: Comes out hours before the decision; the BoJ will see it.
tokyo_cpi.trigger: Prices without fresh food and energy staying at 3% or rising → small push toward Raise.

labour_force_survey.why: Shows whether the job market is still tight.
labour_force_survey.trigger: Small effect on its own. A jump in unemployment → firms up Hold.

minutes_of_the_september_meeti.why: Shows how many members want faster rises.

summary_of_opinions.why: Often the clearest hint about the next meeting.

gdp_july_september.why: Too late for October, but key for December.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil and the Middle East. Brent oil was about $125 a barrel on Oct 6 (FRED). A new jump would raise the chance of a rise. A big drop would make waiting easier.
The yen. The yen was about ¥158 per dollar on Oct 9. A slide well past ¥160 would make imported prices rise faster and push the BoJ to act sooner.
Long-term bond rates. The 10-year rate is about 3%. A sharp further rise would tighten conditions on its own and make the BoJ more cautious; a fall would remove one reason to wait.
Government energy support. Subsidies are holding down household energy prices. Any change to them would move the CPI numbers the BoJ watches.
The Fed. The US Fed raised its rate in September and may raise again. Higher US rates tend to weaken the yen, adding pressure on the BoJ.
A financial shock. A sudden market fall would almost certainly push the BoJ to hold.

report_card.one: Consumer prices look calm, but costs further up the chain are rising fast.
report_card.look: Consumer prices without fresh food (“core CPI”, up 1.7%), without fresh food and energy (up 1.9%), Tokyo prices (up 3.0% without fresh food and energy), and prices businesses pay (up 6.8%).
report_card.why: National consumer prices are slightly below the 2% goal, partly thanks to government energy support. But import prices are up 24.5%, Tokyo prices jumped in September, and the BoJ itself sees a risk that inflation moves above 2%. It is not red because the national number is below target; it is not green because pressure is building.
report_card.change: Core inflation settling near 2% without government support, and import prices cooling as oil falls or the yen strengthens.
report_card.matters: This decides how fast the BoJ raises. If national prices follow Tokyo's jump, a rise comes sooner.

report_card.one: Jobs are plentiful and pay is rising faster than prices.
report_card.look: The unemployment rate, the number of jobs per job seeker, wages, and how hard firms find it to hire (Tankan).
report_card.why: Unemployment is very low at 2.5%. There are 1.18 jobs on offer per job seeker. Wages rose 3.8% in August, and 1.5% after inflation. Firms report a clear shortage of workers. One caution: unemployment ticked up from 2.4%.
report_card.change: Unemployment rising toward 3% or the jobs ratio falling sharply → yellow.
report_card.matters: Strong pay growth is the BoJ's key condition for raising rates. It supports the case for continuing to raise.

report_card.one: The economy is growing, but slowly, and households are not spending more.
report_card.look: GDP (the total value of everything the country produces), household spending, business investment and the BoJ's Tankan business survey.
report_card.why: The economy grew at a 1.4% yearly pace in spring, helped by exports. But household spending was flat and business investment fell 0.9%. Large manufacturers feel better (Tankan score 24), but big firms expect conditions to worsen over the next three months. The BoJ forecasts only 0.6% growth for fiscal 2026.
report_card.change: A weak summer GDP figure on November 16 → closer to red. Stronger spending → green.
report_card.matters: Slow growth is one of the main reasons the BoJ may wait. Members who voted against the September rise pointed to it.

report_card.one: Long-term borrowing costs are high and the yen is weak.
report_card.look: Japanese government bond rates (2-year, 10-year, 30-year), the yen against the dollar, and the BoJ's own description of financial conditions.
report_card.why: Worrying: the 10-year rate is about 3% and the 30-year above 4%, which makes fixed-rate loans much dearer, and the yen is near ¥158 per dollar. Reassuring: the BoJ says financial conditions remain accommodative, and firms still borrow easily.
report_card.change: A disorderly jump in bond rates or a sharp yen fall → red. Calmer bond rates and a steadier yen → green.
report_card.matters: High bond rates argue for patience; a weak yen argues for speed. They pull the BoJ in opposite directions.

consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.what: the government checks the prices of hundreds of everyday things, such as food, rent, energy, clothes and services, and compares them with a year ago. A 1.9% rise means a ¥10,000 basket now costs about ¥10,190.
consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.why: it is very close to the 2% goal. But it is held down by government support for energy bills, so it understates the pressure households feel at the shop.

core_cpi_without_fresh_food.what: CPI without fresh food, whose prices jump with the weather. This is the BoJ's main headline measure.
core_cpi_without_fresh_food.why: at 1.7% it is below 2%. Member Asada pointed to this when he voted against the September rise. The September figure, due October 23, is the key number before the meeting.

cpi_without_fresh_food_and_energy.what: the same check with both fresh food and energy removed, to see the slower trend underneath.
cpi_without_fresh_food_and_energy.why: the yearly rate is near 2%, but the monthly rise of 0.3% is brisk; if it continued for a year, prices would rise more than 3%.

cpi_energy.what: household electricity, gas, gasoline and other fuel prices.
cpi_energy.why: despite high oil prices, household energy prices are slightly lower than a year ago. The BoJ says government measures such as “fuel oil subsidies” are pushing CPI down. If that support is cut, energy prices could jump.

cpi_food_without_fresh_food.what: prices of processed food such as bread, rice dishes and drinks.
cpi_food_without_fresh_food.why: food is what families notice most. Member Masu said “the price of food in general is a key determinant of future inflation.”

tokyo_core_cpi_without_fresh_food.what: the same measure for Tokyo's 23 wards, published about three weeks before the national figure.
tokyo_core_cpi_without_fresh_food.why: it is an early preview of the nation. Part of the jump came from public fees (nursery fees, water charges) and education, not only from businesses raising prices.

tokyo_cpi_without_fresh_food_and_energ.what: Tokyo prices with fresh food and energy removed.
tokyo_cpi_without_fresh_food_and_energ.why: a full point jump in one month. If the national figure follows, the case for a rise in October grows. Services prices in Tokyo rose 2.3%, up from 1.4%.

corporate_goods_price_index_business_p.what: prices that businesses charge each other for goods, such as a factory selling steel or a wholesaler selling fuel.
corporate_goods_price_index_business_p.why: higher business costs usually reach shop prices later. Member Takata expects upstream price rises to “spread to consumer prices downstream.”

import_prices_in_yen.what: what Japanese companies pay, in yen, for goods bought abroad, such as oil, gas and food. In foreign-currency terms the rise was 17.9%.
import_prices_in_yen.why: this is how expensive oil and the weak yen enter Japan's economy. It is the clearest sign of price pressure still to come.

unemployment_rate.what: the share of people who want a job and are looking, but do not have one.
unemployment_rate.why: 2.5% is very low. It means firms must compete for workers, which pushes up pay.

number_of_people_employed.what: how many people have a job.
number_of_people_employed.why: employment rose on a year earlier for the first time in two months. The number of unemployed people (1.80 million) fell for the first time in 13 months.

jobs_per_job_seeker_active_openings_ra.what: how many jobs are on offer at public job centres for each person looking for work.
jobs_per_job_seeker_active_openings_ra.why: above 1 means there are more jobs than job seekers. The ratio for new openings was 2.06, down 0.04 from July, a small sign that hiring demand is cooling.

total_cash_earnings_average_pay.what: average monthly pay per worker, including overtime and bonuses, at firms with 5 or more employees (¥311,364 in August).
total_cash_earnings_average_pay.why: pay rising near 4% a year is consistent with prices rising about 2% over time. This is what the BoJ wants to see.

scheduled_base_pay.what: regular pay without overtime or bonuses.
scheduled_base_pay.why: base pay is “sticky”; once raised, it rarely falls. Steady base-pay growth is the strongest sign that higher prices and wages are becoming normal.

real_wages_pay_after_inflation.what: pay growth minus the rise in prices (using CPI without owners' imputed rent). Using the all-items CPI it was +1.9%.
real_wages_pay_after_inflation.why: households are gaining buying power. That supports spending, and makes it easier for the BoJ to raise rates without hurting families.

spring_wage_talks_shunto_2026_base_pay.what: every spring, big companies and unions agree pay rises. The BoJ says base pay rose by “around 3.5 percent”, about the same as in 2025.
spring_wage_talks_shunto_2026_base_pay.why: these deals set pay for the year ahead. We did not read the union federation's (Rengo) own final tally.

tankan_employment_conditions_all_firms.what: the share of firms saying they have too many workers minus the share saying too few. A negative number means a shortage.
tankan_employment_conditions_all_firms.why: firms expect the shortage to get worse, which keeps upward pressure on wages.

gdp_real_april_june.what: Gross Domestic Product, the total value of everything Japan produces, after removing inflation.
gdp_real_april_june.why: growth is positive but modest. The next figure (summer) arrives on November 16, after the meeting.

household_spending_in_gdp.what: what households spend on goods and services, about half of the economy.
household_spending_in_gdp.why: families are not spending more despite pay rises, probably because prices of food and imports have risen. This argues for patience.

business_investment_in_gdp.what: spending by companies on machines, buildings and software.
business_investment_in_gdp.why: a fall suggests firms were cautious in spring, possibly because of the oil shock.

net_exports_contribution_to_growth.what: how much exports minus imports added to growth.
net_exports_contribution_to_growth.why: exports, helped by AI-related demand and the weak yen, were the main driver of growth in spring.

tankan_large_manufacturers.what: a big BoJ survey of companies. The score is the share saying business is good minus the share saying it is bad.
tankan_large_manufacturers.why: big manufacturers feel better than in June. But they expect a 3-point drop over the next three months.

tankan_large_non_manufacturers.what: the same score for big service companies, such as retailers, hotels and transport.
tankan_large_non_manufacturers.why: still high, but down 2 points, and firms expect a 5-point fall ahead.

tankan_output_prices_large_firms.what: the share of firms saying their selling prices are rising minus those saying falling.
tankan_output_prices_large_firms.why: many firms are still raising prices, which can keep inflation up.

firms_inflation_expectations_all_firms.what: how much firms expect general prices to rise per year.
firms_inflation_expectations_all_firms.why: expectations above 2% mean firms see continued price rises as normal, which the BoJ wants, but not much higher.

boj_forecast_growth_fiscal_2026.what: the middle forecast of the Board members.
boj_forecast_growth_fiscal_2026.why: the BoJ itself expects weak growth this year. A new forecast comes on October 30.

boj_policy_rate_overnight_call_rate_ta.what: the rate at which banks lend to each other overnight, which the BoJ steers. Its deposit rate for banks is also 1.25%, and its lending rate (the “basic loan rate”) is 1.5%.
boj_policy_rate_overnight_call_rate_ta.why: this is the BoJ's main tool. Even at 1.25%, the BoJ describes real interest rates (after inflation) as low.

overnight_call_rate_actual_monthly_ave.what: the actual average overnight rate in the market.
overnight_call_rate_actual_monthly_ave.why: it shows the BoJ's target is being met in practice (the target was about 1.0% then).

2_year_government_bond_rate.what: the interest rate investors demand to lend to the government for two years.
2_year_government_bond_rate.why: at about 1.9%, it is above today's 1.25% BoJ rate, so investors expect the BoJ to keep raising over the next two years.

10_year_government_bond_rate.what: the rate for lending to the government for 10 years. Many fixed-rate loans follow it.
10_year_government_bond_rate.why: about 3% is very high for Japan by recent standards. The monthly average rose from 2.67% in June to 2.94% in August (FRED). Higher long-term rates already cool the economy.

30_year_government_bond_rate.what: the rate for lending to the government for 30 years.
30_year_government_bond_rate.why: very long rates are sensitive to worries about government debt and inflation. Deputy Governor Uchida said bond issuance by AI-related firms has been “putting upward pressure on long-term interest rates.”

10_year_rate_monthly_average.what: the average 10-year rate over each month.
10_year_rate_monthly_average.why: it shows the steady climb in long-term borrowing costs through the summer.

yen_per_us_dollar.what: how many yen it takes to buy one US dollar. A higher number means a weaker yen.
yen_per_us_dollar.why: a weak yen makes imported oil and food more expensive. Governor Ueda says policy does not aim to control the exchange rate, but the BoJ watches its effect on prices.

exchange_rate_assumed_by_big_exporters.what: the rate big manufacturers use in their business plans.
exchange_rate_assumed_by_big_exporters.why: the market rate (about ¥158) is weaker than firms assumed, which boosts exporters' profits but raises import costs.

brent_crude_oil.what: the world's main benchmark price of crude oil. It touched $135.51 on October 2.
brent_crude_oil.why: Japan buys almost all its oil abroad. High oil means higher import costs and, later, higher prices for many goods.

wti_crude_oil_us.why: the gap with Brent (about $29) is unusually large, suggesting supply problems are worse for oil outside the US, such as oil that would normally pass through the Strait of Hormuz.

import_prices_foreign_currency_terms.what: import prices measured in the currencies of the contracts (mostly dollars), so without the yen effect.
import_prices_foreign_currency_terms.why: the gap between this (17.9%) and the yen figure (24.5%) shows how much the weak yen is adding to costs.

petroleum_and_coal_products_business_p.what: prices of fuels sold between businesses in Japan.
petroleum_and_coal_products_business_p.why: still far above a year ago, but the monthly fall is a small sign the energy shock may be peaking.

us_federal_reserve_rate_upper_end.what: the top of the US central bank's target range.
us_federal_reserve_rate_upper_end.why: the gap between US and Japanese rates (about 2.5 to 2.75 points) is one reason the yen is weak.

ecb_deposit_rate_euro_area.what: the main interest rate of the European Central Bank.
ecb_deposit_rate_euro_area.why: other major central banks are also raising rates against the energy shock, so a BoJ rise would not stand out.

said.v: “the Bank will continue to raise the policy interest rate”
w: What it is: the official decision text.
Why it matters: it confirms the direction (up), but gives no timing. It also says “underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2 percent.”

said.v: Asada and Sato voted against the rise
w: What it is: Asada pointed to core CPI “being below 2 percent recently”; Sato said conditions had not “substantially accelerated compared to before.”
Why it matters: two of nine members wanted to wait in September. They are very unlikely to back a second rise six weeks later.

said.v: “bring the policy interest rate closer to the approximate goal relatively soon”
w: What it is: unnamed comments from Board members at the September meeting. Another said: “If signs of an upward deviation in prices are observed, the Bank will need to accelerate the pace of rate hikes.”
Why it matters: some members want to move faster, but conditionally: they want to see prices overshooting first.

said.v: “It does not seem to be accelerating at a speed that could lead the Bank to fall behind the curve,”
w: What it is: a member's view that inflation is not running away. One member also said “the neutral interest rate may deviate upward from prior estimates or the levels anticipated by the market.”
Why it matters: the Board is divided about speed, which favours waiting at the very next meeting.

said.v: Timing and pace will be decided “while checking how likely the central outlook is to materialize and the risks”
said.pv: Sep 18 press conference: no set interval
w: What it is: the Governor's latest public remarks. He also said keeping underlying inflation stable around 2% has become “more important than before.”
Why it matters: the Governor is preparing the public for further rises, but he did not point to October. On September 18 he said there is no fixed pace such as “once every three months.”

said.v: “rate hikes will not be carried out at a fixed pace but will instead be conducted in a nimble and data-dependent manner”
said.pv: Dissented in July for a rise
w: What it is: one of the Board's most hawkish members. He also said “inflationary pressure reflecting the situation in the Middle East could push prices above the target.”
Why it matters: he is likely to support an early rise. One vote cannot decide it.

said.v: “The wage growth rate is a key determinant of monetary policy.”
w: What it is: Masu described underlying inflation as “very close to the 2 percent target” and said the rate should move so that it “falls solidly within the estimated range of the neutral interest rate.”
Why it matters: he supports further rises, without a sense of urgency.

said.v: “it is expected that CPI inflation will move up and stay above 2 percent in the second half of fiscal 2026.”
w: What it is: the BoJ leadership's view of inflation in the coming months. He also said “the Bank should continue to raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary accommodation.”
Why it matters: if national CPI starts rising above 2% as he expects, a rise becomes more likely by December.
What it is: the middle forecast of Board members for CPI without fresh food. Without fresh food and energy: 2.5%, 2.6% and 2.2%.
Why it matters: the BoJ said “There is a risk that it will deviate upward to a level above the price stability target of 2 percent.” Higher forecasts on October 30 would signal a rise soon.

gaps: September national consumer prices (CPI) come out October 23, nine days after this page. Why it matters: this is the most important report before the meeting, so our view may change then.
Market odds for an October BoJ rise. We found no official source for what markets expect. Why it matters: we cannot compare our 27% chance of a rise with market pricing.

Governor Ueda's own words in English. His September 18 press conference and October 6 speech were read in Japanese only; the quotes from them on this page are our translation, not official wording. Why it matters: the Governor's tone is often the best single hint about the next move.
Board member Koeda's speech (October 15) comes after this snapshot. Why it matters: it is one of the last public hints before the meeting.

Daily bond rates for September. The Ministry of Finance history file was too large to load, so we compare October daily rates with monthly averages from FRED instead. Why it matters: we cannot say exactly how far bond rates moved after the September 18 rise.
BoJ underlying inflation measures (trimmed mean, weighted median, mode) could not be read from the BoJ file. Why it matters: the BoJ bases its decisions on “underlying” inflation.

How big the government's energy support is. The BoJ says subsidies and free-education policies push CPI down in fiscal 2026, but we did not find an official estimate of the size, or when the support ends. Why it matters: if support ends, consumer prices could jump quickly.

The Tokyo September jump. The Statistics Bureau attributes much of it to nursery fees, water charges and education; we did not check the policy changes behind those items. Why it matters: one-off fee changes say less about lasting inflation than businesses raising prices.

Board changes. The vote lists show Noguchi Asahi (January) replaced by Asada Toichiro (from April) and Nakagawa Junko (April) replaced by Sato Ayano (from late June). Only 8 members voted in June; we did not check why.

Not collected: industrial production (the METI page did not load), household spending, retail sales, machinery orders, monthly exports, consumer confidence, the Rengo shunto final tally, Dubai crude prices, and any government currency intervention.
How we gathered data: a web search tool was not available for this build. Every number was read directly from the official page linked next to it.

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive. The BoJ's goal is 2% a year, measured by the consumer price index (CPI). It pays most attention to CPI without fresh food (“core CPI”) and to the underlying trend. Note: Japan switched its CPI to a new 2025 base in August 2026.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers show whether people can find work and whether pay is rising. For the BoJ, steady pay rises are the key condition for raising rates, because they let prices rise without making households poorer.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show how fast the economy is growing. A strong economy can handle higher interest rates; a weak one makes the BoJ more careful.
group_intros.rates: These numbers show the BoJ's own rate and the interest rates set by investors. The BoJ sets the very short-term rate; markets set longer-term rates, which matter for fixed-rate home loans and company bonds.
group_intros.said: Official words from the BoJ's statements, meeting summaries and speeches since September. Quotes are exact from the English pages, except Governor Ueda's October 6 speech and September 18 press conference, which we read in Japanese and translated ourselves.
group_intros.global: What is happening outside Japan matters a lot, because Japan imports most of its energy and much of its food, and because the yen reacts to interest rates abroad.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the BoJ has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. FRED carries fewer Japanese series than US ones, and some of them arrive a month or two late. We could not find a FRED series for Japan's consumer prices that is still updated, so CPI is not in this list.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.
